stem: Which statement should a nurse include when teaching an adult about motor-vehicle injury prevention?

options.A: Reserve seat-belt use mainly for highway travel because short local trips have minimal serious-injury risk.
options.B: Adults seated in the rear seat can omit seat belts when the vehicle has front and side airbags.
options.C: Wear a seat belt in every seating position on every trip, no matter how short, because consistent restraint use substantially reduces serious crash-related injury and death.
options.D: Seat belts are primarily a pediatric intervention and add little protection after a passenger reaches adulthood.

rationale: Current CDC guidance states that wearing a seat belt is the most effective way to prevent injury or death in motor-vehicle crashes for adults and older children and that seat belts reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. CDC recommends seat-belt use in front and back seats on every trip, no matter how short, and notes that airbags provide added protection rather than replacing seat belts. Therefore C is correct. A limits use based on trip length, B incorrectly treats airbags as a substitute, and D falsely minimizes adult benefit.
educational_objective: Teach adults to use a seat belt in every seating position on every trip because consistent restraint use substantially reduces serious crash injury and death and remains necessary even with airbags.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Facts About Seat Belt Use; Seat Belts
source_locator: Facts About Seat Belt Use > At a glance/Importance/What you can do: seat belts reduce serious crash-related injuries/deaths by about half; use on every trip no matter how short; airbags are not a substitute. Seat Belts overview: buckle up—every seat, every trip; adult rear-seat use is also important.
source_claim_supported: Adults should wear seat belts in front and rear seating positions on every trip regardless of length; seat belts reduce serious crash-related injury/death substantially and airbags do not replace them.

source_original.stem: Which statement should a nurse include when teaching an adult about motor-vehicle injury prevention?

options.A: Reserve seat-belt use mainly for highway travel because short local trips have minimal serious-injury risk.
options.B: Adults seated in the rear seat can omit seat belts when the vehicle has front and side airbags.
options.C: Wear a seat belt on every trip because consistent restraint use substantially reduces the risk of serious crash-related injury or death.
options.D: Seat belts are primarily a pediatric intervention and add little protection after a passenger reaches adulthood.

source_original.rationale: CDC states that seat belts are the most effective way to prevent injury or death in crashes for adults and older children and that they reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. Consistent use on every trip is recommended.
source_original.source_detail: Seat belts reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths and should be used on every trip. CDC page dated 2026-01-27; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Health Promotion and Maintenance: preventive screening, age/risk-appropriate teaching, developmental and health-promotion activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the seat-belt prevention construct and key C. Tightened C to include every seating position and 'no matter how short,' and explicitly preserved the CDC point that airbags do not replace seat belts.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current CDC transportation-safety guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: CDC Seat Belt pages updated 2026-01-27 and live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: CDC Facts About Seat Belt Use and Seat Belts overview
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses direct CDC prevention statements and does not rely on state-specific seat-belt laws or claim airbags provide no benefit.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because CDC recommends seat belts on every trip regardless of trip length.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because rear-seat adults should buckle up and airbags do not replace seat belts.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because adult seat-belt use substantially reduces crash injury and death.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C accurately reflects the CDC every-seat/every-trip recommendation and adult benefit.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are motor-vehicle safety teaching statements for adults.
audit_findings.blueprint: Health Promotion and Maintenance — injury-prevention education.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current January 2026 CDC seat-belt facts, every-seat/every-trip guidance, airbag statement, all alternatives, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. C remained uniquely correct.
